text: Water enters a plant through its root hair cells by osmosis, moving across selectively permeable membranes from higher to lower water potential.
It then travels through the root into the xylem, where a continuous column of liquid water extends upward toward the leaves.
Inside the leaf, water evaporates from the moist walls of mesophyll cells into tiny air spaces.
The resulting water vapour diffuses through open stomata into the atmosphere.
Evaporation creates tension, or negative pressure, which pulls the remaining water upward through the xylem, against gravity.
Cohesion, caused largely by hydrogen bonds between water molecules, helps maintain the continuous water column.
Adhesion attracts water molecules to the xylem walls.
Guard cells regulate the stomata, balancing carbon dioxide uptake for photosynthesis against water loss.
Together, these processes produce the transpiration stream, carrying water from roots to leaves.
